Droit de la famille — 162274

2016 QCCS 4310

SUPERIOR
COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

N°:

500-12-276934-043

DATE:

July 28, 2016

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF:

THE HONOURABLE

CHRISTIAN J. BROSSARD, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

A.
K.

Plaintiff

v.

R. M.

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(Selection
of school)

______________________________________________________________________

A.

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

X is the 12-year-old daughter of A. K. and V. M..
Next September, she will start her secondary level education.

[
2
]

Divorced for almost ten years, the parents have
so far been able to resolve their disagreements amicably, particularly when it
came to X, whose custody they share.
[1]

[
3
]

Unfortunately, today they strongly differ on an
important issue:  the choice of secondary school for X. They are unable to
resolve the conflict, even in the interest of their child. Indeed, while they
both have their daughter’s best interest at heart, they disagree on what that
interest is:  the father wishes to enrol X at [School A], while the mother
believes that she should attend [School B].

[
4
]

A lawyer was appointed to represent X, so that
the child may express her own wishes through her. However, even though in the
past X has asserted her preference for [School A] to her parents, she no longer
wishes to state a preference. She made it clear to her lawyer that, since her
parents could not agree, she wanted the Court to decide. She did not want to
displease either parent, she wanted to be rid of the stress the issue caused
her and she did not “want to be involved anymore”.

B.

PARTIES’ POSITIONS

[
5
]

Both [School A] and [School B] are private
schools that are fully accredited by the Quebec Government and that comply with
the Quebec curriculum.

[
6
]

The Father argues that they are both excellent
schools and insists that [School A] offers a strong education. X should
therefore be allowed to attend the school of her choice, which, he submits, is [School
A]. He emphasizes his daughter’s passion and talent for the arts and [School A]’
focus on the arts and excellent arts program. [School A] would therefore best
serve X’s need to nurture her creative abilities.

[
7
]

According to the Mother, X has told her that she
would be equally happy at either school. That said, she asserts that [School B]
would be the better school for her daughter, the best “fit” for her, considering
her character, her needs and her aspirations. In particular, she believes that [School
B] offers a stronger academic program and a greater potential for becoming
completely fluent in French, so that it will better prepare X for CEGEP and
university. In addition, [School B] offers Jewish studies and would therefore
be the natural continuation of the Jewish education that X began in elementary
school and that, the Mother emphasizes, her child needs to complete. And X will
be just as able to continue to develop her artistic skills and interests as
part of [School B]’s curriculum and through extracurricular activities.

C.

ANALYSIS

[
8
]

The choice of secondary school is one that falls
under the umbrella of parental authority. Indeed, it is one that would best be left
to the parents, in consultation with their child. However, since the parents
have remained at an impasse despite the Court having fostered their
conciliation after hearing the evidence, it falls upon the latter to decide.

[
9
]

The decision has to be made in the sole interest
of X:

604. In
the case of difficulties relating to the exercise of parental authority, the
person having parental authority may refer the matter to the court, which will
decide
in the interest of the child
after fostering the conciliation of
the parties.
[2]
(Emphasis added.)

[
10
]

Indeed, all decisions that concern a child have
to be taken “in light of the child’s interests and the respect of [her] rights”.
[3]
Consideration has to be given:

[…] in
addition to the moral, intellectual, emotional and physical needs of the child,
to the child’s age, health, personality and family environment, and to the
other aspects of [her] situation.
[4]

[
11
]

That said, the decision is not an easy one. Be
that as it may, based on the evidence, the Court has determined that it would
be in X’s best interest that she be enrolled at [School B].

[
12
]

Here is why.

1.

X’s Wish

[
13
]

The Father asserts that X’s true desire has been
and remains that she be allowed to attend [School A]. Indeed, on a number of
occasions between February and June of 2015, before the Father introduced his
court application on the issue, X stated her preference for [School A],
including in an unaddressed letter dated June 20, 2015 (the GK-1 letter).
[5]
Also, despite having spoken positively about [School B] to her
mother, the child had not demonstrated quite the same enthusiasm as she did for
[School A].

[
14
]

Therefore, the Father urges the Court to accede
to X’s wish, which has not been shown to be against her interest. He argues
that the wish of a 12-year-old child is largely determining in a decision about
herself.

[
15
]

The Mother on the contrary affirms that X has
stated that she would be happy at either [School B] or [School A]. As for the
preference she voiced for [School A] in 2015, it was not based on a fully
informed and mature consideration.

[
16
]

Moreover, while the Mother recognizes that X
should to a degree have a saying in the choice of secondary school, she submits
that it remains the parents’ role to reinforce their child’s strengths and
desires and to steer her in the right direction. In the case of X, the Mother
believes that [School B] would better serve her needs.

1.1.

Applicable Law

[
17
]

The Father relies upon the teachings of the
courts that an informed wish expressed by a child aged 12 or more, freely and
without undue influence, is a largely deciding factor in custody issues.
[6]
Indeed, the strong consideration that is
given to such a wish is based on the belief that a wish so expressed often
corresponds to the child’s interest.
[7]

[
18
]

It is a fact that judges have occasionally
applied
[8]
or considered
[9]
that
precept in the context of a conflict between parents about the choice of school
for their child. That recognises the obligation a court has, when assessing an
application that affects the interest of a child, to:

[…] give
the child an opportunity to be heard if his age and power of discernment permit
it.
[10]

[
19
]

That said, a court is not bound by the child’s
choice if other factors show that it is not in her best interest to follow her
expressed wish.
[11]
In fact, when it comes to issues that would otherwise fall under
the purview of parental authority, such as a choice of school, the legislator
has specifically directed the courts to decide “in the interest of the child”.
[12]

[
20
]

Needless to say, the exercise of parental
authority is not being transferred to the child herself and the choice does not
become hers as a result of her parents being unable to make a joint decision.
The fact is that the child’s best interest will not always correspond to her
desire and that not every wish of a 12-year-old can be granted.
[13]
In the case of a choice of school, courts have sometimes concluded
on a school other than the one preferred by the child.
[14]

1.2.

Discussion

[
21
]

The Court has considered X’s desire, as she
expressed it in 2015. However, it finds that such desire can not be largely
determining or a decisive factor because it was not a wish on the child’s part
that was fully informed and grounded and because today she no longer expresses
a clear and definite preference between [School A] and [School B]. Moreover, as
will be seen later, attending [School B] would be in X’s best interest.

Not a Fully
Informed and Grounded Wish

[
22
]

Both parents testified, as well as X’s paternal
grandfather. The Court also had the benefit of the representations made by the
child’s lawyer. And written proof was filed in the form of X’s GK-1 letter.
That letter however had to be considered under the light of the various
testimonies.

[
23
]

X’s preference for [School A] was based on the
favourable impression it made on her when it came to its arts program and to
the extracurricular activities it had to offer. Indeed, there is no question
that X enjoys arts
[15]
, is even passionate about some forms of art, and that she has a
natural talent for them.

[
24
]

While X is intelligent, articulate and mature
[16]
and while her motivation is not altogether unreasonable from her
point of view, it is not the result of a measured and fully thought-out and
grounded consideration:

1.

One has to keep in mind that X was only an
11-year-old child at the time;

2.

Throughout the process of visiting schools, her
enthusiasm and preference shifted from one school to the next one after each
visit;

3.

X first stated her choice for going to [School
A] before she had visited [School B] and without any knowledge of the latter’s
arts program and of the extracurricular activities it had to offer;

4.

When the Mother questioned X’s reasons for
wanting to attend [School A] and pointed out to her that she needed to wait
until she had visited [School B] and had obtained and considered all of the
information before they could make a decision, X reacted with frustration.
Based on the Mother’s testimony about the conflict that arose at the time
[17]
and on the Father’s description of the circumstances under which
his daughter wrote the GK-1 letter, the Court is convinced that the child wrote
it partly in defiance
[18]
of her mother and out of frustration at seeing her choice and
reasons being challenged;

5.

X’s statement in her GK-1 letter that “I was
dreaming to go to [[School A]] ever since I was little” was not true
[19]
;

6.

X’s motivation was limited to the arts program
and extracurricular activities without considering other important factors such
as the strength of the academic programs and general education; and

7.

The Father’s testimony has convinced the Court
that X was to a degree influenced by her father’s own enthusiasm about [School
A] (albeit through no bad faith on the part of the Father, possibly even
unintentionally).

Lack of a
Clear and Definite Preference

[
25
]

In July of 2015, X took a step back from her
previously stated choice for [School A]. At the time, the disagreement between
her parents had made its way to court. She told her mother the subject of the
choice of school was stressing her, she had decided not to be involved with the
decision, she recognized that her parents were in the best position to decide
what was best for her and, whether it was [School A] or [School B], she knew
she was going to be happy at either place.

[
26
]

One year later, in June of 2016, between two
meetings with her lawyer, X answered “No” when her father asked if she would
like him to drop his court application so she would go to [School B]. Yet, she
unequivocally told her lawyer, in anticipation of the court hearing, that she
liked both schools and had no preference and that she wanted the judge to
decide.

[
27
]

Whether X has become ambivalent about her desire
or she simply wishes to avoid displeasing either parent and to avert the stress
of having to make a choice, the fact is that she is not being assertive,
certain or definite about a choice of school.

[
28
]

As for pressure put on X by the Mother so that
she would state a preference for [School B], through bribery or coercion, as
alleged by the Father, it has not been proven. The Father relies upon
inadmissible hearsay evidence, namely statements made by X to her father and
grandfather, in the first half of 2015, about things that the Mother would have
said to her and about a “cold treatment” she would have gotten from her
mother’s husband. While the fact that the child made the statements is
admissible evidence, those statements are not admissible evidence as to the
truth of what X reported about her mother and the latter’s husband. They did
not pass the test of reliability.
[20]

[
29
]

Even if the evidence had been admissible, the
Court finds that the child’s untested statements must give way before the
Mother’s denials, which have a much stronger probative value. The Court
concludes that X’s statements were not accurate and were those of an
11-year-old child who had misconstrued and possibly distorted what her mother
had said. In all likelihood, at the time, X was overcome or carried away by a
degree of frustration with her mother at being unable to convince her of the
adequacy or strength of her reasons for preferring [School A] over [School B].
It is very unlikely, improbable, that the Mother would have tried to “bribe” or
coerce X or done anything that would constitute unseemly or disproportionate
pressure on her daughter. That assessment considers the family history since
the parents’ divorce, the Mother’s testimony in general, the explanations she
gave in particular about her discussions with X, and her demeanour when
testifying.

* *

[
30
]

In the end, the evidence leads to the conclusion
that X would not be unhappy at either [School A] or [School B].

2.

X’s Best Interest

[
31
]

The Father submits that the two schools are
equivalent in terms of their academic programs and that, in the end, the choice
is between a school that has a particular focus on the arts, [School A], and
one that devotes a large portion of its curriculum to Jewish studies, [School
B].

[
32
]

The Father believes that [School A] would be
better suited to X’s creative abilities and passion for arts, because, although
not an arts school, it promotes creative expression and is known for its
excellent arts program.

[
33
]

Moreover, the Father asserts that as a result of
her elementary schooling, X has had, and feels that she has had, sufficient
Jewish education, which she has also expressed to her paternal grandfather.

[
34
]

The evidence convinces the Court otherwise.

2.1.

Quality of Education

[
35
]

According to the parents, X currently aspires to
become a radiologist, more specifically a neuroradiologist, while also becoming
a professional hip-hop dancer (although possibly on her “spare time”
[21]
). Of course, no one knows for certain what post-secondary education
and career path X will actually follow. That is not the issue. The issue is to
determine whether one of the two schools, taking into consideration X’s goals,
abilities, capabilities and character, will provide her with a better secondary
level education and will prepare her better for CEGEP and university, so that
she may then make her own choices.

[
36
]

In addition to written proof being filed about
both schools’ curriculum and achievements, the Court had the benefit of hearing
from [School B]’s President and [School A] Director of Admissions about their
respective schools and their mission, core values, priorities, curriculum and
academic program, objectives and achievements,
[22]

approach to French language studies, arts program, extracurricular activities,
faculty and clientele.

[
37
]

Also, the Mother described the need for her
daughter, a bright and hardworking student who enjoys sciences and maths, to be
challenged and pushed, in a structured and rigorous academic environment, in
order to excel to a level commensurate with her abilities and ambitions.

[
38
]

Based on the descriptions of the two schools and
of what they each have to offer, the Court was left with the impression, indeed
with a belief that, while they both offer academic and general education of a
high standard, similar in some respects, [School B] is a step above and would
best respond to X’s needs.

[
39
]

Moreover, perhaps more importantly, the Mother,
who obviously has a clear and carefully considered understanding of her
daughter’s character and ensuing needs, has made a convincing argument, under
the light of the testimonies from the two school officials, that [School B] is
better suited to X’s needs.
[23]

2.2.

Arts

[
40
]

[School A] may have an excellent arts program.
However, the Court is satisfied by the evidence that, whether X attends [School
B] or [School A], she will be able to continue to develop her artistic skills
and to “fulfill that part of her identity”:
[24]

1.

Arts
[25]
is
one of four “pillars” on which [School B]’s strategic plan is built and it
offers a fair range of opportunities to engage one’s artistic interests, both
as part of its curriculum and as extracurricular activities; and

2.

The Mother has always supported X and respected
her choices when it came to gymnastics, ballet, hip-hop dancing, piano, visual
arts, drama, in short nurturing and encouraging the artistic side of her
personality, and she intends to continue to do so.

2.3.

Jewish Studies

[
41
]

At the time of the divorce, the parents agreed
that X would receive Jewish education as part of her elementary level schooling
and would attend a Jewish private elementary school. They did not provide for
the secondary level schooling in their agreement. Today, the Mother wants X to
continue her Jewish education as part of her schooling, while the Father wants
her to attend a non-denominational school.

[
42
]

In addition to its secular general studies
education, [School B] also provides Jewish education as one of its four
pillars, “Jewish Ethics and Litteracy”.

[
43
]

Both parents are Jewish. The Father described
himself as a secular Jew who is not very observant of religious rituals and
whose observance of Jewish holidays is cultural rather than religious. The Mother
explained that she is fairly observant, as she was throughout the marriage, yet
not ultraorthodox by any means. In the context of joint custody, the foregoing
translates into X being more observant of the Jewish religious and cultural
traditions, rituals and ceremonies when she is with her mother than when she is
with her father.

[
44
]

From the Mother’s clear, detailed, confident and
unequivocal testimony, the Court was convinced of X’s happiness throughout her
elementary schooling in a Jewish school, of the importance of religion to her,
of her continued interest in her Jewish identity and her religious practice and
curiosity about Jewish religion, and of her willing, eager and enthusiastic
participation in religious rituals and ceremonies. On some level, that was
corroborated by the Father, who talked about X’s recent decision to eat only
kosher meat, and by the child’s grandfather, who described her as having a
strong Jewish identity (even though not totally orthodox).

[
45
]

That said, the Mother presented a convincing
argument that X’s Jewish education was not complete from having done her
elementary schooling at a Jewish school and that Jewish studies as part of her
secondary level schooling would provide her with the complete education that would
then allow her to make her own choices. The after-school (possibly weekly)
[26]
program that the Father proposed would not provide X with an
equivalent education.

[
46
]

That said, the Court does not believe that the
Mother aims to keep X in a “Jewish bubble”, as the Father has argued. And the
testimony of [School B]’s President has convinced the Court that it is not an
objective of the school either nor is it an unavoidable consequence of the
school’s Jewish studies and student body.
[27]

Rather, X would be in an environment that offers a balance between the secular
general studies and the Jewish studies, that proposes different perspectives,
that encourages its students to develop a critical mind and analytical thinking
as part of question-based studies, that teaches them to make their own choices
and that promotes diversity.

2.4.

Conclusion

[
47
]

In short, studying at [School B] would allow X
to continue her Jewish education, in a school that offers secular general
studies education of a high standard and that meets her needs, while still
allowing her to develop her interests and abilities in arts. At the same time,
attending [School B] would make it easier for the parents and their daughter to
continue joint custody of X between a secular Jewish father and a more
observant Jewish mother.

[
48
]

Since X will be starting her school year in just
a few weeks and is currently enrolled tentatively in two schools, an order of
provisional execution is appropriate.

3.

School Costs and Tax Deductions

[
49
]

The parents have agreed to share the costs of X
attending [School B].

[
50
]

As part of her address to the Court, the Mother
has asked that the agreement made at the time of the divorce be modified so
that the available tax benefits and credits regarding X be shared by the
parties on an equal basis. That may be justified, however, as the Father
rightfully argued in reply, no application was properly and timely made by the
Mother, no evidence was submitted, and any decision on the subject by the Court
would be rendered
ultra petita
.

[
51
]

That said, the Court urges the parties to
resolve that particular issue amicably, as they have done on other issues over
the last ten years.

4.

X’s Lawyer’s Fees

[
52
]

The legal costs related to the representation of
a child are to be decided according to the circumstances.
[28]

[
53
]

Despite the Mother’s belief that X did not want
to have a lawyer appointed to her and despite the child’s choice not to state a
preference for a school to her lawyer, the fact is that a lawyer was appointed,
with the court’s authorization, so as to elucidate the child’s desire and that
the lawyer played a useful role at the hearing. There is no reason why the
parents should not share the fees equally, as suggested by the Father.

[
54
]

X’s lawyer’s fees shall be borne equally by the
parents.

FOR THOSE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
55
]

DISMISSES
the
Father, the plaintiff A. K.’s
Motion to Modify Accessory Measures
;

[
56
]

DECLARES
that the
minor child X shall attend [School B] for her secondary level education (so long
as she continues to meet the school’s requirements) beginning at the start of
the 2016-2017 school year, unless otherwise agreed to (in writing) by the
parties, and
ORDERS
the parties to act accordingly;

[
57
]

PRAYS ACT
of the
parties’ agreement to share the costs of X attending [School B] and
ORDERS

them to comply with the agreement;

[
58
]

PRAYS ACT
of the
parties’ undertaking not to discuss the proceedings with X;

[
59
]

PRAYS ACT
of the
parties’ undertaking to accept the decision of the courts regarding the school,
unless otherwise agreed to (in writing) by the parties, and not to be critical
of the decision in the presence of X;

[
60
]

ORDERS

provisional execution of the foregoing conclusions;

[
61
]

ORDERS
the
parties to pay the professional fees and disbursements of M
tre
Orna
E. Hilburger as lawyer for X, in equal proportions.
